phonemes.desc: Close front vowel [i], lightly stressed in the first syllable of the divine name.
Alveolar nasal [n] flanked by open vowels [a], giving the name its characteristic resonance.
Final open syllable with reduced stress; in Sumerian, the doubling of the nasal is orthographic rather than phonemic.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ee-NAHN-nah' — stress the second syllable, keep the vowels bright, and let the double n sound like a held tongue against the ridge.

pronunciation.note: The Sumerian name is written in cuneiform as 𒀭𒈹. The ASCII form inanna flattens the name to lowercase and removes the proper-noun marking; the restoration Inanna recovers the standard scholarly citation form. Because the restoration adds only the conventional capital of a proper name, the entry is placed in Tier 2.

domains.title: Lady of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Love, War, and the Morning Star
domains.lead: Inanna is the Sumerian great goddess whose domain stretches across the heavens and the human heart. She is the planet Venus as both morning and evening star, the force of sexual desire and fertility, the frenzy of battle, and the sovereign power that legitimises kings. No other deity of ancient Mesopotamia so thoroughly refuses to be one thing: she is the lover and the warrior, the bride and the conqueror, the star that crosses from the eastern to the western horizon and back again.

cards.name: The Morning Star
cards.desc: Venus in the dawn sky; Inanna is the celestial sign whose rising marks time, royalty, and the renewal of desire.

cards.name: Love and Fertility
cards.desc: Sacred marriage, reproductive power, and the life-giving force that turns desire into offspring and fields into harvest.

cards.name: Divine Warfare
cards.desc: She rides into battle with weapons at her shoulders; kings invoke her as patron of campaigns and conquest.

cards.name: Sovereignty
cards.desc: The goddess who bestows and withdraws kingship; her favour is the divine charter of Sumerian rulers.

symbols.name: Eight-pointed star
symbols.meaning: The sign of Venus, her planet; the star disk crowns her tiara and writes her name in cuneiform.

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her warlike aspect and royal mount; she stands upon lions as mistress of battle.

symbols.name: Reed bundle
symbols.meaning: The cuneiform sign 𒈹 that writes her name, a stylised bundle of reeds linking her to the marshes of Sumer.

symbols.name: Rosette
symbols.meaning: The fertility emblem attached to her cult from the Uruk-period cylinder seals onward.

mythology.lead: Inanna's myths are stories of extremity and transformation. She descends into the underworld, demands the impossible, and returns from death. She chooses a shepherd-king as her bridegroom and then sends him to the realm of the dead for half the year. Her narratives are not morality tales; they are meditations on sovereignty, desire, death, and the price of rebirth.

myths.title: Inanna's Descent to the Netherworld
myths.text: In the Sumerian Descent of Inanna (ETCSL c.1.4.1), the goddess abandons heaven and earth to descend to the netherworld ruled by her sister Ereškigal. At each of the seven gates the gatekeeper Neti strips her of a garment or ornament — crown, scepter, beads — until she stands naked before the throne of the dead. Ereškigal fixes on her the eye of death; Inanna is killed and hung on a hook. Her faithful servant Ninšubur, waiting at the gate, pleads with Enlil and Nanna and is refused; Enki answers, creating from the dirt of his fingernails two beings, gala-tura and kur-jara, fashioned without male or female parts, who slip past the underworld's guardians and revive her with the food and water of life. But the judges of the dead will not let her go free: someone must take her place, and the one she finds sitting unmourned on her throne is Dumuzi. The myth is a meditation on death, sovereignty, and the price of rebirth: she who went below returns with the dead man's shadow attached to her, and the underworld keeps its claim.

myths.title: Inanna and Dumuzi
myths.text: The sacred-marriage songs celebrate the union of Inanna and Dumuzi, the shepherd-king: 'my honey-man, my honey-man sweetens me always', runs one of the bridal hymns of Uruk, among the earliest love poetry known. Their lovemaking ensures the fertility of the land and the legitimacy of the king, whose reign was ritually ratified as the goddess's marriage. In the Descent, however, the bride becomes the judge: Inanna fastens on Dumuzi the eye of death and sends him below for half the year, while his devoted sister Geštinanna offers to share the doom, so the two alternate, each six months in the realm of the dead. The myth explains the cycle of the seasons and the alternating presence of life and death in the agricultural year — but it also refuses the sentimental reading: the same desire that raises the king to his throne hands him over to the pit.

myths.title: The Huluppu Tree
myths.text: The tale survives fragmentarily, on school tablets of the Old Babylonian period, and was reconstructed by S. N. Kramer from its broken lines. Inanna plants a huluppu tree — a willow-like species, unidentified — in her holy garden at Uruk, and tends it for the throne and bed she means to cut from its trunk. But three beings take it: the serpent 'who could not be charmed', the storm-bird Anzu, and the dark maid Lilith (the ki-sikil-lil-la-ke of the Sumerian). Inanna appeals to Gilgameh: the hero slays the serpent with his axe, and the bird and the maid flee into the desolate places. From the freed wood Inanna fashions her throne and bed — the furniture of sovereignty. The story links the goddess to kingship, the civilising of wild nature, and the dangerous thresholds between order and chaos; its heroines and monsters were still moving westward three thousand years later, when the Lilith of this tale surfaced in Talmudic and Kabbalistic legend.

myths.title: The Theft of the Me
myths.text: In Inanna and Enki (ETCSL c.1.3.1), the goddess sails the Boat of Heaven to Eridu to visit her father Enki, the god of wisdom. He receives her with a banquet; the beer and wine flow, Enki grows merry, and to each toast he grants a gift — the me, the divine powers and norms that constitute civilization: kingship, priesthood, truth, the crafts, the making of music, sexual arts, and the rules of city life, over a hundred of them. When Enki sobers and regrets his largesse, the me are already loaded on Inanna's boat and bound for Uruk. He sends the monsters of sea and land to seize the cargo; one after another they bar the way, and Inanna answers each with cunning until the Boat of Heaven reaches her city, where she is acclaimed. Enki concedes at last: 'What has been spoken cannot be unsaid.' The myth is Uruk's charter of cultural primacy — wisdom walks out of Eridu as a party trick — and its heroine's method is the point: civilization is not guarded by the wisest but seized by the boldest.

myths.title: Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta
myths.text: In the epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta (ETCSL c.1.8.2.3), Inanna favours the king of Uruk and supports his campaign to subdue the legendary city of Aratta, whose lord commands the mountains and claims the goddess for his own. The two kings trade riddling challenges through a messenger, and Enmerkar, guided by dreams and by Inanna's counsel, presses his rival to submission without a single battle in the surviving text. The tale dramatises her role as divine patron of kings and the strategic advantage conferred by her cult centre at Uruk: a king with Inanna's ear holds, in effect, the ear of heaven. Its interest for readers is the portrait of sovereignty it assumes — power resolved by wit, message, and divine favour more than by the sword — with the goddess as the umpire both kings must persuade.

etymology.derivation: The name is transparently Sumerian: nin 'lady' + an 'heaven' + ak (genitive case marker). It is one of the few major Mesopotamian divine names whose etymology is certain. The Akkadian form Ištar, which eventually supplanted Inanna in speech, is of Semitic origin and probably represents a conflation with a separate Venus deity.

nameVariations.note: Standard Sumerian spelling used in scholarly and literary sources.
Akkadian form that absorbed Inanna's cult from the Old Akkadian period onward.
West Semitic cognate, the Levantine Venus goddess.
Plain ASCII fallback; a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling.

lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform as 𒀭𒈹 — the divine determinative 𒀭 plus the reed-bundle sign 𒈹 read Inanna. The Unicode restoration Inanna is a scholarly transliteration rather than the original script; the cuneiform form is not registrable in the .com IDN table. Because the restoration adds only the conventional capital of a proper name, it is classed Tier 2.
lore.syncretism: Inanna was so thoroughly identified with the Akkadian Ištar from the Old Akkadian period onward that the two are now treated as a single deity across most of Mesopotamian history. Through Ištar she was equated with the West Semitic Astarte, the Hurrian Šauška, and the Egyptian Qudshu, and she contributed features to the Iranian goddess Anāhitā. The Greeks identified her with Aphrodítē in her eastern, armed form. In the Hebrew Bible, her star and cult shadow the 'Queen of Heaven' denounced by Jeremiah.
lore.culturalLegacy: Inanna's afterlife is inseparable from that of Ištar/Astarte. Her eight-pointed star persists in Near Eastern and occult symbolism, and her Descent has been read as a precursor to later underworld journeys from Orpheus to Christ. In modern scholarship she has become a central figure in feminist re-readings of ancient religion, admired for her autonomous sexuality and her refusal to accept the limits imposed by gods or mortals. Her sacred-marriage hymns, some of the earliest love poetry known, continue to be translated and performed.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Inanna asks us to hold opposites together. She is the morning star and the evening star, the bride and the warrior, the goddess who descends into death and returns clothed in her own power. In a world that likes its deities sorted by function, she is a reminder that the most ancient sacred forces were polymorphous: desire and violence, fertility and mourning, all braided into a single brilliant light.

To restore the name Inanna is to refuse the flattening of the feminine divine into mere beauty or mere nurturing. She is the terror of the battlefield and the tenderness of the bridal chamber; the goddess who weeps for the flood's victims and sends the Bull of Heaven to avenge her pride. Her star still rises.

lore.archaeology: The Eanna precinct at Uruk — 'House of Heaven' — preserves the sequence of Inanna temples from the Uruk period onward, source of the archaic cylinder seals that first display her star, lion, and rosette. Thousands of personal names, royal inscriptions, and incantations attest her presence in daily religion from the third millennium to the last generations of cuneiform scribes.
